paragraphs.text: When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. (“Minefield” may be misleading; there were also secret pits filled with spikes.) The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed!

During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. As he reached for the door, he almost triggered the first booby trap: a fishing line wrapped around the handle that was attached to a rigged shotgun cartridge. Suddenly the contents of the house looked rather different. If one door had been trapped, any of them might be. So might any of the shoulder-high piles surrounding him.
